Compute the coordinates of nodes

Source: R/layout_networks.R
layout_networks.Rd

A network has no natural position on a page. Force-directed layouts place nodes so that tied nodes are close and untied nodes are pushed apart, so that clusters appear as dense regions: Kamada-Kawai ("kk") draws graph distances as geometric distances (Kamada and Kawai 1989) , Fruchterman-Reingold ("fr") balances attraction along edges and repulsion between all nodes (Fruchterman and Reingold 1991) . layout_networks() computes such coordinates with ggraph::create_layout(), which gives access to the layouts of igraph and graphlayouts, and stores them in the node table. Two layouts that are not in ggraph are added: "forceatlas2" (Jacomy et al. 2014) , the force-directed layout of Gephi, and "umap" (McInnes et al. 2018) , which embeds the distances between nodes with the UMAP algorithm.

For a list of networks, the coordinates of a node may jump from one window to the next, which makes the plots hard to compare. With compute_dynamic_coordinates = TRUE, the coordinates of window \(t-1\) are used as the starting positions of the layout of window \(t\), so that the nodes present in both windows tend to stay in the same region.

Usage

layout_networks(
  graphs,
  node_id,
  layout,
  compute_dynamic_coordinates = FALSE,
  save_coordinates = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

graphs

A tbl_graph or a list of tbl_graphs.

node_id

Character scalar, the node column with a unique identifier, used to join the coordinates.

layout

Character scalar, a layout accepted by ggraph::create_layout() (e.g. "kk", "fr", "stress"), or "forceatlas2" or "umap" (see the details).

compute_dynamic_coordinates

Logical. For a list of graphs, if TRUE, each layout starts from the coordinates of the previous window (see the details).

save_coordinates

Logical. If TRUE, the coordinates are also stored in x_{layout} and y_{layout} (e.g. x_kk, y_kk), so that they are not lost when another layout is computed.

...

Other arguments of the layout (see ggraph::create_layout() and the igraph or graphlayouts function behind it; the arguments of "forceatlas2" and "umap" are given in the details).

Value

The same object as graphs, with node columns x and y (any existing x and y are replaced) and, if save_coordinates = TRUE, x_{layout} and y_{layout}.

Details

Force-directed layouts are stochastic and sensitive to the starting positions: set a seed with set.seed() before calling the function to reproduce a figure. Distances in such plots are only roughly interpretable: two clusters drawn side by side are more tied than two clusters at opposite ends, but distances should not be measured.

Weights. igraph uses the weight edge column automatically, but not always in the same way: Fruchterman-Reingold ("fr") reads weights as attraction (heavier edges pull nodes closer), while Kamada-Kawai ("kk") reads them as distances, so that similarity weights push the most similar nodes apart and weakly tied nodes to the margins. With similarity weights, prefer "fr", or pass weights = NA to ignore them.

ForceAtlas2 (layout = "forceatlas2"). A force-directed layout of the same family as Fruchterman-Reingold, designed for the exploration of networks (Jacomy et al. 2014) . Edges attract their ends in proportion to their weight and to the distance; all nodes repel each other in proportion to the product of their degrees plus one, so that hubs push the others away and clusters separate; a gravity keeps the components around the centre. The speed adapts to the stability of the forces. This is a compact implementation, not the one of Gephi: the repulsion is computed between all the pairs of nodes (no Barnes-Hut approximation), so that the cost grows with the square of the number of nodes (comfortable up to a few thousand). Arguments: iterations (500), scaling_ratio (2, the strength of the repulsion: smaller values give a more compact layout), gravity (1), strong_gravity (FALSE; TRUE keeps disconnected components close), linlog (FALSE; TRUE uses a logarithmic attraction, which separates the clusters more) and weights (the edge column is used by default, divided by its maximum; NA ignores it). Isolated components drift away from the rest: keep the main component with filter_components() first, or use strong_gravity = TRUE.

UMAP (layout = "umap"). UMAP (McInnes et al. 2018) places points in the plane so as to preserve their neighbourhoods. It needs distances between all the pairs of nodes, which a network does not give directly: the distance between two nodes is the length of the shortest path between them, an edge being as long as the inverse of its weight (a strong tie is a short one), and nodes of different components are set farther apart than any connected pair. The coordinates come from uwot::umap(). Arguments: n_neighbors (15, the size of the neighbourhood preserved: larger values give a more global view), min_dist (0.1, how tightly nodes are packed), spread (1) and weights (as above), and any other argument of uwot::umap(). The package uwot must be installed. UMAP often gives compact, well separated clusters, but, like the force-directed layouts, its distances are not to be measured, and the picture is partly built by the choice of n_neighbors.

For dynamic coordinates, nodes absent from the previous window start at (0, 0). The starting positions are passed to the layout as its coords argument: this works only with layouts that accept it, such as "fr" and "kk" of igraph, and "forceatlas2"; "umap" ignores them.

References

Fruchterman TMJ, Reingold EM (1991). “Graph Drawing by Force-Directed Placement.” Software: Practice and Experience, 21(11), 1129–1164. doi:10.1002/spe.4380211102 .

Jacomy M, Venturini T, Heymann S, Bastian M (2014). “ForceAtlas2, a Continuous Graph Layout Algorithm for Handy Network Visualization Designed for the Gephi Software.” PLoS ONE, 9(6), e98679. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0098679 .

Kamada T, Kawai S (1989). “An Algorithm for Drawing General Undirected Graphs.” Information Processing Letters, 31(1), 7–15. doi:10.1016/0020-0190(89)90102-6 .

McInnes L, Healy J, Melville J (2018). “UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction.” doi:10.48550/arXiv.1802.03426 . 1802.03426.

Examples

network <- build_network(
  nodes = subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation"),
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  method = "similarity",
  edges_threshold = 2
)
#> ℹ Coupling (`biblionetwork::biblio_coupling()`) with "similarity": ties
#>   weighted by the idf-weighted cosine of the two lists of targets, after Shen
#>   et al. (2019), between source_id entities sharing target_id entities.
#> ℹ Pairs sharing fewer than 2 target_id are dropped (`edges_threshold`).
#> ℹ Nodes without any edge are removed (`keep_singleton = FALSE`).
set.seed(1)
network <- layout_networks(network, node_id = "source_id", layout = "fr")
head(tidygraph::as_tibble(network, active = "nodes")[c("source_id", "x", "y")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   source_id      x     y
#>   <chr>      <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 96284971   -4.27 -2.09
#> 2 37095547  -14.1  -6.22
#> 3 46282251  -13.5  -7.26
#> 4 214927     -4.60 -7.96
#> 5 2207578    -6.95 -4.36
#> 6 10729971   -3.53 -5.94
